lines.text: Great lakes and the highest mountain in Africa, the footprints of our ancestors, a spice coast and a young union. This is the story of Tanzania.
About ten million years ago, the Rift Valley began to hold Lake Tanganyika, long and deep, home to hundreds of fish found nowhere else.
Some three point seven million years ago, early human relatives walked upright across wet volcanic ash at Laetoli, and their footprints are still there.
Kilimanjaro rose from the plains, a snow-capped volcano almost six thousand metres high, the roof of Africa.
About two million years ago, a great volcano collapsed into itself, leaving the Ngorongoro Crater, now crowded with lions and elephants.
Far younger is Lake Victoria, the largest lake in Africa by area, shared with Uganda and Kenya, and the source of the White Nile.
From about the year 800, on the island of Kilwa, a town grew that would become the richest on the Swahili coast.
Its sultans grew wealthy on the Indian Ocean trade in gold and ivory, and built stone mosques and a palace, until Portugal attacked in 1505.
Along this coast, Swahili took shape, a Bantu language rich in Arabic words. Today it is shared across Tanzania, Kenya and beyond.
In the nineteenth century, Omani sultans ruled Zanzibar, a great centre of the spice and slave trade.
In 1862 a new town was founded on the mainland coast, Dar es Salaam, today the country's largest city.
In 1885 Germany claimed the mainland as German East Africa, a colony that also took in Rwanda and Burundi.
In 1896 Britain fought Zanzibar in the shortest war in history, over in well under an hour.
In 1905 the peoples of the south rose against German rule in the Maji Maji rebellion, a great revolt that was put down by force.
Julius Nyerere was born in 1922. A teacher, he would lead his country to independence and become its first president.
From 1931, at Olduvai Gorge, the Leakey family searched the rocks, and found early human fossils and stone tools.
In 1946 a boy was born in Zanzibar who would become Freddie Mercury, the singer of Queen.
Two years later, Abdulrazak Gurnah was born in Zanzibar. As a novelist, he would win the Nobel Prize in 2021.
In 1951 the Serengeti became a national park, famous for the yearly march of wildebeest and zebra across its plains.
John Magufuli, born in 1959, would be elected president in 2015 and die in office six years later.
His deputy, Samia Suluhu Hassan, born in Zanzibar in 1960, would then become the first woman president.
Tanganyika became free in 1961. Then, in 1964, a revolution on Zanzibar overthrew the sultan.
Within months, Tanganyika and Zanzibar united, and the new country took the name Tanzania.
In 1967 Nyerere set out the Arusha Declaration, his plan for African socialism and self-reliance.
In 1978 Idi Amin's Uganda attacked, and Tanzania struck back. By 1979 Amin had been driven out.
And in October 2025, a general election was marred by protests in which people were killed.
From the footprints at Laetoli to a nation of many peoples, Tanzania's story continues.
